problems.prompt: Two concepts were both marked learned a month ago. One has been reviewed three times since, spaced out; the other has not been touched since the day it was learned. Which one's mastery estimate has likely decayed further by today?

choices.text: The one reviewed three times, because more reviews means more practice fatigue
The one never reviewed again — a full month with nothing renewing it lets it fade the most
Both decay by exactly the same amount, since decay depends only on how long ago it was learned
Neither has decayed — once a concept crosses the learned threshold it stays there

problems.solution: Memory strength decays over time without practice, and each spaced review resets and extends that decay. The concept with three reviews has had its forgetting curve reset three times since; the untouched one has had a full month to fade unopposed.

problems.prompt: A concept was learned yesterday. Why does the app schedule its first review for a few days out, instead of either drilling it again immediately or waiting a month?

choices.text: Immediately would be too easy to test anything, and a month would be so late the concept had already faded past the threshold and had to be relearned — the app aims for the point where recall takes real effort but still succeeds
It reviews on a fixed weekly schedule for every concept, regardless of when it was learned
It waits until the learner explicitly asks for a review
It only reviews concepts the learner got wrong, never ones just learned

problems.solution: Spaced repetition aims each review at the point on the forgetting curve where recall is difficult but still likely to succeed — too soon wastes the review on something you still remember easily; too late lets the concept lapse and forces a relearn instead of a reinforcement.
